title: Eternal rest
hook: eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessing children: a parent's thumb drawing a small cross before sleep. Your line was a cross on the forehead. Who got a blessing from you, in whatever form? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

A small card, the size of a playing card, left on a table at the back of a funeral home. On the front, a painting of Jesus or Mary. On the back, a name, two dates, and four short lines. People slip these cards into wallets, Bibles and kitchen drawers, and find them again years later, a little bent at the corners. The four lines are often the same, whoever's name is above them. Catholics say them for the famous and the forgotten alike. Today, the prayer on the back of the card.
screen: `A CARD AT THE BACK OF THE FUNERAL HOME.` → `A NAME, TWO DATES, FOUR LINES.` → `THE SAME LINES FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here are the lines, in their traditional English form. "Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. May they rest in peace. Amen." First, the word. In Latin the prayer opens "Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine." Requiem is the Latin for rest. Those same words open the entrance chant of the Church's Mass for the dead, and that Mass, and music written for it, carry the name requiem. Second, the two gifts it asks for. Rest, after a life of work and worry. And light, after the dark of death. Not light for a moment, perpetual light, light that doesn't go out. Notice that the prayer asks nothing for the person saying it. It is entirely for someone else. Third, why Catholics pray for the dead at all. They point to the second book of Maccabees, where Judas Maccabeus has prayers and sacrifice offered for fallen soldiers. The Douay-Rheims closes the passage this way: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." The Catechism teaches that those who die in God's friendship but still need purifying can be helped by the prayers of the living. Not every church counts Maccabees as scripture, or prays for the dead in this way, and that difference can be named plainly. Last, look back at this week. Pilgrims at Lourdes and Fatima, your local shrine, the incorruptibles, a votive candle, grace before meals, a cross on a child's forehead. Again and again, someone was held up to God: the sick, a stranger, a child. Today's prayer is the same gesture, offered for people who can no longer ask for anything themselves.
screen: `REQUIEM IS THE LATIN FOR REST.` · `REST AND LIGHT, ASKED FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` · `A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT.` · `A WEEK OF HOLDING PEOPLE UP.` · then, large: `LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray it for your dead. Settle, and breathe. Let one name come to mind, someone who has died. A grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, someone you barely knew but haven't forgotten. Say the name quietly. If you pray, you can say the four lines for them: eternal rest, perpetual light, rest in peace, amen. Then let another name come, and another, as many as arrive. If you don't pray, say each name and leave a breath of quiet after it, like a candle left burning. The bell holds the time.
Requiem. Latin for rest, the first word of the Church's prayer for the dead and of the entrance chant at a Mass for the dead. Today's word.

Your line: let perpetual light shine. Today, when a name of someone who has died crosses your mind, give it the line, or a moment of quiet, before you move on. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Catholics say the Eternal Rest prayer for the dead at funerals, at graves, during November, after grace or the rosary, and whenever a person who has died is remembered. It is often printed on the back of funeral prayer cards.

notes: Week end: the teach looks back at days 1387–1392 (Lourdes and Fatima, local shrine, incorruptibles, votive candles, grace before meals, blessing children).

Traditional English text of the Eternal Rest prayer: confirm wording (some versions read 'and let perpetual light shine upon them. May they rest in peace. Amen.'; some add the line for the souls of the faithful departed).

Claim that the Requiem Mass took its name from the opening word of its introit ('Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine'), and that musical settings took the name from the Mass: standard, but confirm phrasing.

CCC 1030–1032 paraphrased: those who die in God's grace and friendship but imperfectly purified undergo purification; the Church commends prayer for the dead. 'Other Christians read death and prayer differently' is deliberately unspecific; a Keeper may prefer naming that many Protestant churches do not pray for the dead in this way, or leaving it out.
Funeral prayer cards: described as a custom, with 'often' for the prayer on the back; confirm acceptable.

Editor pass: cut 'older than English' and 'every one of their dead'; removed the causal history of the name requiem from the teach; reframed other churches fairly (not every church counts Maccabees as scripture); softened the week look-back (the incorruptibles day was not a prayer for someone).
